tactic.name: Prioritize Agentics
tactic.one_liner: Spend the majority of your engineering time on the agentic layer — the ring of prompts, template meta prompts, and AI developer workflows wrapped around your codebase — because every hour invested there teaches compute to do the application-layer work for you.
tactic.why_uncomfortable: It demands you stop doing the very work that feels most productive. Writing application code, fixing the bug yourself, shipping the feature by hand — all of it is now, by default, the wrong layer. Dan's rule of thumb is that at least half your engineering time (more when bootstrapping) goes to infrastructure that doesn't ship user-visible value directly, on the promise that the return is parabolic: 10 minutes in, two hours out. And it carries a humbling corollary: 'Do not make the mistake of thinking you're smarter than your best engineering practices templated into your agentic layer' — you must trust the encoded system over your in-the-moment self, because a template meta prompt running in an ADW that kicks off five to ten agents per problem will out-execute you.
tactic.compresses_all_tactics: Dan states this tactic 'has been staring us in the face the entire time' and 'represents all others, from target zero-touch engineering all the way back to stop coding. All tactics are compressed into this tactic.'

mission: Close the loop on TAC: cement the primitives (prompts up through ADWs) as tool-agnostic building blocks, walk four working agentic layers hands-on so you have concrete V1 starting points, then compress every KPI, leverage point, and tactic into one daily guiding question — 'Am I working on the agentic layer or the application layer?' — and send you off to build the system that builds the system.

agentic_layer.definition_dan_words: "What is the agentic layer? It is the combination of traditional deterministic code that is stored in your ADWs directory as a scriptable layer that combines deterministic code with the new non-deterministic agentic technology — the language model, the agent, Claude Code, and whatever variants are gonna come next. You combine these two things. This makes up your agentic layer, the old world of deterministic code and the new world of agentic prompts." (~50:20)
agentic_layer.ring_metaphor: Imagine a ring around your codebase. At first it's thin, then it becomes thicker as you scale agentics into your codebase — machines that operate with your judgment, shipping your way, getting work done autonomously in your product. (~1:05; visualized on screen as a green pixel ring)
agentic_layer.vs_application_layer: Two layers only. The application layer is deliberately vague — DevOps, infrastructure, database, and the raw application all live under it. The agentic layer is the separate, isolated ring (prompts + ADWs + plans) that operates ON the application layer. Dan is emphatic about the separation: 'Our application and our agents — they're distinctly different… keep it isolated and separated. This is not the application layer.'
agentic_layer.time_allocation: As a general rule at least half of your engineering time goes to the agentic layer (more up-front when building it initially); the ratio fluctuates but the more you invest, the more problem classes the layer solves on your behalf. (~4:00)
agentic_layer.parabolic_roi: "When you have a product that you're maintaining, building an agentic layer is parabolic… put 10 minutes in, get two hours of value out or more." It starts thin and not very useful; value compounds as you add ADWs, template your engineering, and always add feedback loops so agents can ship and auto-improve. (~15:38)
agentic_layer.micro_codebase_warning: As it scales, the agentic layer becomes its own micro codebase — a wrangle layer around your codebase — so apply real engineering patterns to it, while keeping it separated from apps/. (~27:45)

guiding_question.question: Am I working on the agentic layer or am I working in the application layer?
guiding_question.framing: Revealed at ~52:39 as 'the final question… a final meta tactic' and earlier teased as 'the oil of this course' (~2:14) — all Agentic KPIs, every leverage point, and all eight tactics compress into it. 'Even if you forget all eight tactics, this is all you need to think about.'
guiding_question.right_answer: The majority of your time should be on the agentic layer, because you can teach compute how to build, teach compute how to engineer your way, and scale compute beyond comprehension — orchestrating intelligence.
acceptable_reasons_for_application_layer: You're running your prompts in the loop specifically to verify they'll work out of the loop
guiding_question.otherwise: "Or else you're moving in the wrong direction. You're going sideways while other engineers… will be moving up."

pieces: adws/ — AI Developer Workflow directory: scripts that fuse deterministic code with agent calls (the highest abstraction level)
.claude/commands/ — your prompts as markdown slash commands (using Claude Code; any prompt store works)
specs/ — plans: the markdown output of planning prompts that implementation prompts consume
minimum_viable_agentic_layer.scripting_layer_rule: Any scripting layer works — UV single-file Python scripts (used throughout TAC), Bun if you like TypeScript, shell if you're old school. The ONLY requirements: you can compose code, reference other files, and keep it isolated from the application layer.
minimum_viable_agentic_layer.starter_prompts: A /prime command to set the agent up (standalone, reusable, with different priming variants per codebase section), a /start command to boot your app (uv run + bun run here, as complex as needed), /chore + /feature template meta prompts to plan, and /implement (a higher-order prompt taking a plan as its argument) to build.
minimum_viable_agentic_layer.quote: "For your minimum viable agentic layer, you really only need these pieces." (~7:00, over tac8_app1's README)

core_concepts.name: Tactic #8: Prioritize Agentics
core_concepts.plain_english: The final tactic and the compression of all seven before it: direct your engineering time at the agentic layer, not the application layer. It drives daily ROI decisions — every task you do by hand is a problem class you failed to teach your agents.
core_concepts.dan_words: "It's simple. It's everything. Prioritize agentics. More specifically, prioritize your agentic layer." (~3:16)
core_concepts.misconception: That prioritizing agentics means neglecting your product. Dan closes the loop explicitly: 'By investing in your agentic layer, you're actually investing in your application layer — it's all about your users, your product, and your company. Never forget who this is all for.'

core_concepts.name: The two-layer model of a codebase
core_concepts.plain_english: Every codebase now has exactly two layers that matter: the application layer (app, database, infra, DevOps — everything classical) and the agentic layer (prompts, templates, plans, ADWs, triggers) that operates on it. The layers must stay physically separated — apps/ in its own directory that the agentic ring operates around.
core_concepts.dan_words: "There's the agentic layer, and then there's the application layer… I recommend more than half of your time should be focused on the agentic layer." (~3:50–4:31)
core_concepts.misconception: Treating the agentic layer as part of the app (mixing agent scripts into application code). The isolation is the point: the same agentic-layer shape wraps ANY application layer — a Jupyter data-science app (app2), a Vue observability dashboard (app3), a prototyping factory (app4), a FastAPI+Vite product (app5).

core_concepts.name: Keep your eyes on the primitives
core_concepts.plain_english: The composable units — individual agentic prompts up to composed multi-step ADWs — are what matters. Not the software developer lifecycle, not a model, not a tool, not Claude Code. Tools are the current vehicle; the primitives transfer.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Claude Code represents the first viable engineering tool that unlocks agentic engineering… but it won't be the last. We know tools will change and models will improve. We can't fixate on these… I've talked very little on Claude Code specifically — this is very intentional. This is not a Claude Code course." (~5:00–6:00)
core_concepts.misconception: That TAC's value expires with its tooling. The whole lesson is built to survive tool churn: every codebase teaches prompt/plan/template/ADW composition that any agent runtime can execute.

core_concepts.name: The Minimum Viable Agentic Layer (MVAL)
core_concepts.plain_english: Three directories bootstrap everything: prompts (.claude/commands/), plans (specs/), workflows (adws/). app1 (tac8_app1__agent_layer_primitives) is a nearly-empty codebase shipping exactly this starting point plus a two-file apps/ layer to operate on.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This is the minimum set of pieces of information that you need… The only thing that matters is that you can compose code and reference other files and have this be isolated from your application layer." (~7:00–7:40)
core_concepts.misconception: That you need the scaled version (hooks, triggers, state, worktrees, observability) on day one. app1's README shows both shapes — minimum viable and scaled — and the lesson's order is explicit: start thin, thicken the ring as value compounds.

core_concepts.name: The gateway script (adw_prompt.py)
core_concepts.plain_english: A single script that takes a prompt string, calls one Claude Code instance programmatically, and manages all the surrounding state — unique ADW ID, output capture to agents/{adw_id}/{agent_name}/ as JSONL stream → JSON array → final object → custom summary. It is the smallest possible ADW and the on-ramp to everything else.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This script is the gateway into agentic coding… It's the minimal version of what you need to get started. This ADW is calling an agent — this is distinctly different from any other type of code." (~13:39)
core_concepts.misconception: That it's a trivial wrapper. The 'surrounding state' IS the value: reproducible IDs, streamed logs you can tail, a final object you can parse, and a summary you can build yourself — the observability layer that later multi-agent systems depend on.

core_concepts.name: Template meta prompts (prompts that generate prompts)
core_concepts.plain_english: Markdown prompts (/chore, /feature, /plan, /plan_uv_mcp…) that take a high-level request plus an adw_id and output a PLAN in a rigidly specified 'Plan Format' — metadata, description, relevant files, step-by-step tasks executed top to bottom, and validation commands. The plan file is itself a prompt for /implement. This is how you template your engineering.
core_concepts.dan_words: "These are meta prompts. They template out what your engineering workflows look like… Do not underestimate the plan format… This is a prompt that generates a prompt." (~9:49–11:10)
core_concepts.misconception: That the general /plan is the end state. It's the floor: 'You will be able to outperform these by going more specific' — app4's /plan_uv_mcp, /plan_vite_vue, /plan_uv_script, /plan_bun_scripts each encode framework-specific expertise plus ai_docs references, which is why one concise prompt can produce a working MCP server.

core_concepts.name: Solve problem classes, not one-off fixes
core_concepts.plain_english: The unit of agentic-layer work is the CLASS of problems (all chores, all MCP-server builds, all data-set updates), not the instance. Templating the engineering pattern once means every future instance is a one-line prompt.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We're focusing on problem classes, not one-off fixes… I have solved the problem class of building Astral UV model context protocol servers. I've solved it. It's done." (~10:50 and ~38:50)
core_concepts.misconception: Writing a prompt so specific it solves only today's task. The tell that you templated a class: a teammate (or an agent) can run it against a request you never anticipated and get your team's engineering standards in the output.

core_concepts.name: In-loop → out-loop: a great place to start, a terrible place to stay
core_concepts.plain_english: The maturity ladder inside every codebase in this lesson: (1) type prompts in a Claude Code session (in-loop), (2) fire the same prompts via ADW scripts (slightly out-loop, no conversation, no responding), (3) let triggers — cron, task files, Notion boards, embedded servers — fire the ADWs without you (out-loop), (4) target ZTE where even review drops away.
core_concepts.dan_words: "By creating a script that can surround the application… we are slowly moving out the loop. I'm not responding here. I'm not having a conversation with the agent… [In-loop] is a great place to start. It's a great place to do deep work… It's a terrible place to stay. So many engineers are going to miss this mark." (~15:00–15:25)
core_concepts.misconception: That out-loop means abandoning in-loop entirely. Dan runs /prime and /start in-loop on camera first — in-loop remains where you build and debug the agentic layer itself; it's the place you operate FROM, not the place work ships from.

core_concepts.name: Triggers + a two-way task file = a multi-agent system in one or two files
core_concepts.plain_english: app2's whole orchestration layer is a cron trigger polling tasks.md every 5 seconds. The markdown file is a two-way interface: humans write tasks grouped under '## Git Worktree <name>' headers with optional {tags}; agents rewrite the same lines through states [] → [🟡, adw_id] → [✅ commit_hash, adw_id] or [❌, adw_id] // Failed: reason, with [⏰] tasks blocked until every task above them succeeds. Tags flip behavior: {opus} upgrades the model, {adw_plan_implement_update_task} upgrades the workflow from build-update to plan-implement-update.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Every five seconds, our trigger is going to pick up on tasks that need to be operated… It found seven tasks to kick off… I'm not doing this by the way — this is all our ADWs and our agents starting to pick up work… We're pushing past the overkilled chat-based UI. We have a two-way task list." (~21:48–23:30)
core_concepts.misconception: That multi-agent requires heavy infrastructure. 'This is a small tweak. This is one or two files… and all of a sudden we're able to do a lot more with a multi-agent dedicated workspace system.' The trigger itself delegates parsing to a /process_tasks prompt that returns eligible task groups as JSON — the agent is the parser.

core_concepts.name: Git worktrees with sparse checkout as agent environments
core_concepts.plain_english: Each worktree name in tasks.md becomes trees/<name> — a real git worktree on its own branch with sparse checkout of ONLY the target app directory, .env copied in, and an empty initial commit. Every agent gets an entire isolated copy of the environment for exactly its set of work; parallel experiments (perfect for data-science variants) can't collide.
core_concepts.dan_words: "These are dedicated environments for agents to work in… we have a sparse checkout of just this directory… an entire copy of this environment of this codebase for this agent to do just this set of work in." (~22:00, ~28:37)
core_concepts.misconception: That isolation is only for safety. It's also for THROUGHPUT (5 worktrees × parallel agents) and for review ergonomics — Dan opens trees/enhance-training-data as its own editor window, greps tweets_positive_only.csv, and validates one agent's work without touching the others.

core_concepts.name: PITER applied: Prompt input, Trigger, Environment, Review
core_concepts.plain_english: The lesson-7 out-loop framework recurs in every codebase here. app4 names it explicitly: Prompt input = the Notion page; Trigger = adw_trigger_cron_notion_tasks.py polling every 15 seconds; Environment = dedicated worktrees under trees/; Review = the board's Human-in-the-loop column plus live status updates written back to the task page.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Remember the PITER framework. You have prompt input — for us, it's this Notion page. Environment — this is going to operate inside the trees directory… And then we have the review system." (~30:54)
core_concepts.misconception: That the review system must be a dashboard. It's whatever surface you already look at: a Notion board on your phone, the tasks.md diff, the worktree in your editor, or (app5) a chat window inside your own product.

core_concepts.name: One agent, one prompt, one purpose — and its single exception
core_concepts.plain_english: The controversial rule for reliability under small context windows: each Claude Code instance runs exactly one prompt for one purpose, making agents focused, reproducible, testable, and improvable. Across every TAC codebase there is exactly one exception: app5's AEA server passes the stored cc_session_id back with --resume to continue a conversation, because an embedded product agent needs conversational continuity.
core_concepts.dan_words: "One agent, one prompt, one purpose… We're running one Claude Code instance with only one exception… where we are actually passing back in the session ID back into this agent to continue the conversation. Every other prompt we ran, we have one agent, one prompt, one purpose." (~47:53–48:36)
core_concepts.misconception: Hearing 'one purpose' as 'one tool call' or 'tiny prompts'. The purpose can be as large as 'implement this whole plan' — what's prohibited is the sprawling multi-topic conversation whose context window becomes unreproducible.

core_concepts.name: From PITER to PITE: drop the R
core_concepts.plain_english: The ZTE end-state restated for the agentic layer: once a dialed-in ADW ships end-to-end reliably, human review becomes the bottleneck — so you remove it. Prompt input, trigger, environment… no review. It happens gradually (small chores first), and only because you always added feedback loops and taught agents a concrete review step (images, videos, multi-step review ADWs).
core_concepts.dan_words: "You realize you're the bottleneck and then you'll convert the out-loop framework from PITER to PITE… You'll drop the R off… Not only will you stay out the loop — getting in the loop will be harmful. You will let your product ship itself." (~49:21–50:15)
core_concepts.misconception: That dropping review is recklessness. The sequence is strict: feedback loops first ('There is a validation, a set of validations in your codebase that once run ensures everything works perfectly — the only question is, do you know what it is?'), then reliability streaks, THEN removing yourself.

core_concepts.name: AEA: the agent embedded in the application
core_concepts.plain_english: app5 breaks the layer-separation rule on purpose: a FastAPI 'AEA server' (port 8743) lives inside the ADW triggers directory, persists agents in SQLite (agent_id, cc_session_id, conversation), and the product's own UI opens chat windows (Cmd+P → /aea) where named agents (Nexus, Roon on camera) answer questions about the codebase and ship changes to the running app. Out-loop, here, means INSIDE the application.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We have an agent inside of our app… The power of agents isn't in one, it's in many… How does this work? We broke one of our rules… We have a dedicated agent embedded application server so that we can access this outside the loop. In this case, outside the loop is inside the application." (~40:18–42:00)
core_concepts.misconception: That AEA is a chatbot feature. It's presentational scaffolding for a bigger idea: 'You can make your own fully built out agents inside your application that can operate your domain… better and faster than you or any engineer on your team can.' The demo agent literally edits the app's own button while chatting.

core_concepts.name: The commoditization of implementation
core_concepts.plain_english: Phase-1 commoditized code; the agentic layer commoditizes IMPLEMENTATION — the whole act of turning intent into shipped changes — with early signs of commoditizing engineering itself. Value moves up the stack: system design, architecture, encoding domain expertise for agents, quality control and validation review systems, and above all creative problem decomposition, which you then encode into ADWs.
core_concepts.dan_words: "AI coding is not enough. With agentic coding, not only is code a commodity, but the implementation as well. This is only a net negative if you show up late to the party. You are here very early… The value of engineering is actively moving up the stack." (~56:39–57:30)
core_concepts.misconception: Reading this as doom. Dan frames it as asymmetric opportunity — 'This is bigger than a course. This is a manifesto for the next phase of software engineering… the codex for agentic engineering' — for those who internalize it early.

twelve_leverage_points_recap.note: Printed verbatim in app1's and app2's READMEs as the course's canonical list; the lesson recaps them at ~11:38 and ~44:00 with ADWs named 'the highest level of composition — code plus agentics.'

agentic_kpis_recap.attempts: Decrease the attempts it takes to deliver work with your agents
agentic_kpis_recap.size: Increase the size of work you can hand off
agentic_kpis_recap.streak: Increase the streak of successful work shipped without mistakes
agentic_kpis_recap.presence: Drop your presence — showing up to prompt, review, babysit — to the bare minimum, target zero (stay out the loop)

tactics_recap_all_eight: 1. Stop coding — 'the irreplaceable engineer of the future is not writing a single line of code' (~43:34)
2. Adopt your agent's perspective — build with the core four (context, model, prompt, tools) so agents have what they need
3. (12 leverage points) Layer them on and hand them to your agent at the right time in the right place — in-agent and through-agent
4. Template your engineering — template meta prompts: prompts that output prompts with specific formats, rules, files to read, conditional docs
5. Increase your Agentic KPIs — attempts down, size up, streak up, presence to zero
6. Always add feedback loops — validation commands agents run to confirm their own work; 'the big three Gen AI companies… have these insane feedback loops… you can do this on your codebase' (~47:14)
7. Target zero-touch engineering — the North Star; PITER loses its R as reliability compounds
8. Prioritize agentics — the meta-tactic that contains them all

four_codebases.teaches: The minimum viable agentic layer, piece by piece: prompts (/prime, /start, /chore, /feature, /implement), the gateway ADW (adw_prompt.py), slash-command ADW (adw_slash_command.py), the first composed ADW (adw_chore_implement.py: /chore → extract plan path → /implement), plus SDK variants (agent_sdk.py, adw_sdk_prompt.py). Application layer is deliberately trivial: apps/main.py + apps/main.ts printing 'Hello, agentic coding world!'.

four_codebases.teaches: Multi-agent 'Todone' (to-do → to-DONE) task delegation: tasks.md as a two-way emoji-state task board grouped by git worktree, a 5-second cron trigger, /process_tasks returning eligible work as JSON, /mark_in_progress + /update_task rewriting states, /init_worktree building sparse-checkout worktrees under trees/, and two workflow tiers (adw_build_update_task.py default; adw_plan_implement_update_task.py via tag). Application layer: a Jupyter sentiment-classification project over tweets_v1.csv.

four_codebases.teaches: Skipped on camera ('I'll let you open that up on your own'). It is the multi-agent observability system: Claude Code hooks (pre/post tool use, notification, stop, subagent stop, user prompt submit) POSTing events through send_event.py to a Bun+SQLite server with a Vue 3 live dashboard (WebSocket stream, pulse chart, chat transcripts). The agentic-layer lesson embedded in it: observability is what makes fleets of out-loop agents reviewable.

Fully out-loop rapid prototyping driven from a Notion board: a 15-second cron trigger picks up tasks with 'execute' triggers, claims them ('In progress' + adw_id), generates worktree names (/make_worktree_name), creates isolated worktrees, routes {{prototype: uv_script|vite_vue|bun_scripts|uv_mcp}} tags to specialized template meta prompts (/plan_uv_mcp etc. + ai_docs/), implements, and writes results back to Notion (statuses: Not started / In progress / HIL Review / Failed / Done; iterate via 'continue - <prompt>'). Agents spawn as detached subprocesses so the monitor never blocks.

A FastAPI AEA server (port 8743, SQLite persistence of agent_id/cc_session_id/conversation) launches adw_aea_patch.py per prompt; the client dev console (Cmd+P: /aea, /list, /toggle-view, /close-all) opens chat windows with named agents that answer codebase questions and implement changes, resuming sessions via --resume. The one sanctioned exception to one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose.

quotes.text: Imagine a ring around your codebase. At first it's thin, then it becomes thicker as you scale agentics into your codebase. Machines that operate with your judgment, shipping your way, getting work done autonomously in your product.
This guiding question represents the oil of this course. All the Agentic KPIs, every tactic, it compresses all of it into a single question.
Prioritize agentics. This tactic has been staring us in the face the entire time.
As a good starting point, I recommend half of your engineering time, at least half, should be spent on the new agentic layer.
Keep your eyes on the primitives… It's the primitives, right? Claude Code represents the first viable engineering tool that unlocks agentic engineering… but it won't be the last.
The only thing that matters is that you can compose code and reference other files and have this be isolated from your application layer.
These are meta prompts. They template out what your engineering workflows look like… This is a prompt that generates a prompt.
This script is the gateway into agentic coding… This ADW is calling an agent. This is distinctly different from any other type of code.
By creating a script that can surround the application, that can surround any unit of code, we are slowly moving out the loop.
It's a great place to start. It's a great place to do deep work… It's a terrible place to stay, okay? So many engineers are going to miss this mark.
Building an agentic layer is parabolic. It's absolutely parabolic. Put 10 minutes in, get two hours of value out or more.

Remember: prioritize agentics. Prioritize the agentic layer of your codebase. Don't do the work by yourself. Teach your agents to do it. Teach them how to solve the problem class. Build the system that builds the system.
You will get to a point where your ADWs, in combination with your prompts, is its own kind of micro codebase — a wrangle layer around your codebase.
I have solved the problem class of building Astral UV model context protocol servers. I've solved it. It's done.
The power of agents isn't in one, it's in many.
One agent, one prompt, one purpose… This creates focused agents, focused context windows, that are reproducible and easily testable, validatable, and improvable.
You realize you're the bottleneck and then you'll convert the out-loop framework from PITER to PITE… You'll drop the R off… You will let your product ship itself.

Don't make the mistake of thinking that you can outperform your team's best engineering practices encoded into a template metaprompt that runs in an AI developer workflow that kicks off five to ten agents per problem.
Am I working on the agentic layer or am I working in the application layer? That's it. On a day-to-day tactical level, even if you forget all eight tactics, this is all you need to think about.
There is no competing with an agentic engineer. You must have fleets of agents operating on your behalf to compete with an agentic engineer.
An agentic engineer operates on living pieces of software that work while they sleep.
What we're seeing here… is the commoditization of implementation and early signs of the commoditization of engineering.
This is bigger than a course. This is a manifesto for the next phase of software engineering… the codex for agentic engineering.
When the agents arrived, something changed. We weren't just AI coding anymore. We started orchestrating intelligence.

prerequisites_tools: TAC lessons 1–7 (this lesson recaps and compresses all prior tactics, KPIs, and leverage points)
Claude Code with API funds or a plan (ADWs run with --dangerously-skip-permissions in programmatic mode; ANTHROPIC_API_KEY via .env)
Python + UV (all ADWs are uv single-file scripts with inline dependency blocks)
Bun (app1 /start, app3 server/client, app4 bun prototypes) and Node.js 18+
Git with worktree support (app2/app4/app5 isolation) and the GitHub CLI for app5's issue-driven ADWs

Optional per app: Notion account + @notionhq/notion-mcp-server via .mcp.json and NOTION_AGENTIC_TASK_TABLE_ID (app4); OpenAI/Anthropic keys for the NLQ-to-SQL app; ElevenLabs/OpenAI keys for app3 TTS hooks
An IDE (Dan uses VS Code windows per worktree: `code trees/<name>`)
what_student_must_internalize: Every codebase has two layers now: the application layer (everything classical) and the agentic layer (prompts + plans + ADWs + triggers) that operates on it — and they must stay physically separated.
Tactic #8 contains all others: prioritize agentics. At least half your engineering time on the agentic layer; the return is parabolic (10 minutes in → 2 hours out).
The minimum viable agentic layer is three directories: .claude/commands/ (prompts), specs/ (plans), adws/ (workflows) — in any scripting language that can compose code and reference files.

An ADW is deterministic code that calls agents: the gateway script (one prompt, managed state, structured outputs under agents/{adw_id}/) is the seed; composition (chore→implement, build→update, plan→implement→update) is the growth pattern.

Template meta prompts ARE templated engineering: a Plan Format with step-by-step tasks and validation commands turns your best practices into a reusable artifact; specialize them per problem class (/plan_uv_mcp beats /plan for MCP servers).
Solve problem classes, not one-offs — the test is whether one concise prompt now produces an entire correct artifact (Dan: an MCP server end to end).
In-loop is for building and debugging the agentic layer; work ships from out-loop. The ladder: prompt → slash command → ADW script → trigger (cron/task-file/board/embedded server) → ZTE.

A two-way task file plus a cron trigger is a complete multi-agent system: states [] / [⏰] / [🟡, adw_id] / [✅ hash, adw_id] / [❌, adw_id], tags ({opus}, {adw_plan_implement_update_task}) as per-task config, worktrees with sparse checkout as dedicated agent environments.
PITER structures every out-loop system (prompt input, trigger, environment, review) — and the ZTE end-state is PITE: you drop the R once feedback loops and streaks prove you're the bottleneck.

One agent, one prompt, one purpose — reproducible, testable context windows; the sole exception in all of TAC is app5's session resume (--resume with a stored cc_session_id) for the in-app conversational agent.
Always add feedback loops: your codebase already has a set of validations that proves everything works — the only question is whether you know what it is; encode it so agents can self-verify.
The daily compass: 'Am I working on the agentic layer or the application layer?' Application-layer work needs a reason (deadline, testing, in-loop verification of prompts) or you're moving sideways.

Implementation is being commoditized; your value moves up the stack — system design, domain encoding, quality control, creative problem decomposition — all of which you then encode into your agentic layer.
common_weak_student_failures: Nodding at the ratio, then spending 100% of the week in the application layer 'just to hit the deadline' — never bootstrapping the layer that would have hit the next ten deadlines. The tactic is a time-allocation change, not a belief.
Cloning tac-8 and reading the code instead of RUNNING it: the lesson's value is watching a trigger pick up work you didn't dispatch by hand ('I'm not doing this by the way').

Building prompts but no ADW directory — staying a prompt collector. If you're only operating with prompts, you're missing out on tons of capabilities; the fusion of deterministic code with prompts IS the layer.

Copy-pasting Dan's directory shapes as gospel. He says the opposite three times: 'this is just an arbitrary agentic layer… you can build it any way you want' — the invariants are isolation, composability, observability, feedback loops.
Mixing the layers: agent scripts inside apps/, or agents writing directly to main without worktrees — then concluding multi-agent 'doesn't work' when parallel edits collide.

Skipping the tags/blocking semantics in tasks.md and writing one giant task — never seeing dependencies (⏰), model upgrades ({opus}), or workflow routing ({adw_plan_implement_update_task}) that make the board a real orchestrator.

Treating one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose as optional and building a sprawling conversational mega-agent — losing reproducibility and testability, the exact failure the rule prevents (context windows are still small).
Dropping review before adding feedback loops — PITE without validation commands is not zero-touch engineering, it's unsupervised risk. The R is REPLACED by encoded review, never merely deleted.

Fixating on the exact tools (Claude Code flags, Notion, VS Code) instead of the primitives — the lesson explicitly de-emphasizes Claude Code, and 'don't fixate on the exact details, focus on the agentic layer.'
Answering the guiding question honestly but only once. It's a DAILY question — 'every day when you sit down to work' — not a course-completion checkbox.
teach_back_prompt: Explain to a colleague, without notes: (1) what the agentic layer is — Dan's exact two-ingredient definition — and how it differs from the application layer; (2) the minimum viable agentic layer's three pieces and why isolation from apps/ is non-negotiable; (3) how tac8_app1's adw_chore_implement.py fuses deterministic code with two agentic prompts, including how the plan path travels from /chore's output into /implement's argument; (4) how tasks.md + a 5-second cron trigger becomes a multi-agent system — walk the emoji state machine and what {opus} and {adw_plan_implement_update_task} tags do; (5) the one exception to one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose and why it's justified; and (6) the final guiding question, the three acceptable reasons to be in the application layer, and why Dan calls the layer's ROI parabolic.

retrieval_questions.q: What is Tactic #8, and what does Dan say it contains?
retrieval_questions.a: Prioritize agentics — prioritize your agentic layer. It represents and compresses ALL other tactics, 'from target zero-touch engineering all the way back to stop coding.'

retrieval_questions.q: Define the agentic layer in Dan's two-ingredient formulation.
retrieval_questions.a: Traditional deterministic code (stored in your ADWs directory as a scriptable layer) combined with the new non-deterministic agentic technology (the language model / agent, e.g. Claude Code and its successors). Old world of code + new world of agentic prompts.

retrieval_questions.q: What are the three pieces of the minimum viable agentic layer, and the one rule about the scripting layer?
retrieval_questions.a: An adws/ AI-developer-workflow directory, prompts (.claude/commands/), and plans (specs/). Any scripting language qualifies (UV Python, Bun TS, shell) as long as you can compose code, reference other files, and keep it isolated from the application layer.

retrieval_questions.q: How much engineering time does Dan recommend for the agentic layer, and what's the stated ROI shape?
retrieval_questions.a: At least half — more when bootstrapping. The ROI is parabolic: put 10 minutes in, get two hours (or more) of value out.

retrieval_questions.q: What is 'the gateway script' and what does it manage beyond calling the agent?
retrieval_questions.a: adw_prompt.py — a UV single-file ADW that runs one adhoc Claude Code prompt. It manages the surrounding state: a unique ADW ID, retry logic, and structured outputs under agents/{adw_id}/{agent_name}/ (raw JSONL stream, JSON array, final object, custom summary).

retrieval_questions.q: Walk the emoji state machine of app2's tasks.md, including blocking.
retrieval_questions.a: [] pending → [🟡, adw_id] in progress → [✅ commit_hash, adw_id] success or [❌, adw_id] … // Failed: reason. [⏰] tasks are blocked and only become eligible when EVERY task above them in the same worktree is ✅; a ❌ above permanently blocks them.

retrieval_questions.q: What do the task tags {opus} and {adw_plan_implement_update_task} do?
retrieval_questions.a: {opus} upgrades the model for that task (default sonnet); {adw_plan_implement_update_task} routes the task from the default build-update workflow (/build → /update_task) to the full plan-implement-update workflow (/plan → /implement → /update_task).

retrieval_questions.q: How does a plan travel through adw_chore_implement.py?
retrieval_questions.a: Phase 1 runs /chore with [adw_id, prompt]; the planner agent writes specs/chore-{adw_id}-{name}.md and reports the path; the script regex-extracts that path from the agent's output and passes it as the argument to /implement, which the builder agent executes.

retrieval_questions.q: How do agents get isolated environments in app2/app4, mechanically?
retrieval_questions.a: /init_worktree creates trees/<name> via git worktree add --no-checkout on a new branch, configures cone sparse-checkout of only the target app directory, checks out, copies .env in, and makes an empty initial commit — a dedicated per-agent copy of just the relevant slice.

retrieval_questions.q: Map PITER onto app4's prototyping system.
retrieval_questions.a: Prompt input = the Notion task page; Trigger = adw_trigger_cron_notion_tasks.py polling every 15 seconds (with --once for testing); Environment = sparse-checkout worktrees under trees/; Review = the board's columns (Not started / In progress / HIL Review / Failed / Done) plus live status updates written back to Notion.

retrieval_questions.q: State the one-agent rule and the single exception in all of TAC.
retrieval_questions.a: One agent, one prompt, one purpose — focused, reproducible, testable context windows. The only exception is app5's AEA system, which stores cc_session_id in SQLite and passes it back with --resume so the in-app agent can hold a conversation.

retrieval_questions.q: What is PITER-to-PITE, and what must exist before you drop the R?
retrieval_questions.a: The ZTE conversion: once a dialed-in ADW ships end-to-end and review stops catching anything, you remove the Review step (Prompt input, Trigger, Environment). Prerequisites: you always added feedback loops (validation commands agents run) and taught agents a concrete review step — the R is replaced by encoded review, not deleted.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the final guiding question, and the three acceptable reasons to answer 'application layer'?
retrieval_questions.a: 'Am I working on the agentic layer or am I working in the application layer?' Acceptable application-layer reasons: a deadline, testing something, or running prompts in-loop specifically to verify they'll work out-loop.

retrieval_questions.q: What did one concise prompt produce in app4's demo, and what does Dan conclude from it?
retrieval_questions.a: A complete, working Astral-UV Python MCP server (system info: get_memory_info, get_cpu, get_disk) planned by /plan_uv_mcp with ai_docs references, built in an isolated worktree, wired via .mcp.json. Conclusion: 'I have solved the problem class of building Astral UV MCP servers' — template meta prompts turn classes of engineering into one-prompt operations.

what_each_does.tac8_app2__multi_agent_todone/adws/adw_m: Pydantic models for the board: Task, Worktree, WorktreeTaskGroup, ProcessTasksResponse, CronTriggerConfig, and SystemTag (extracts model/workflow choices from {tags}).

current_practice_gaps.why: tac-8 encodes every reusable behavior as .claude/commands/*.md invoked by name from ADWs. Current Claude Code packages reusable expertise as Agent Skills (SKILL.md with frontmatter, trigger descriptions, on-demand loading, shareable across repos/teams) — the modern answer to 'template your engineering.' The lesson's meta-prompt concept maps 1:1; the packaging and discovery upgraded.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Hand-rolled subprocess agent.py → Claude Agent SDK
current_practice_gaps.why: Every app copies a ~630-line agent.py that shells out to `claude -p --output-format stream-json` and hand-parses JSONL. Dan already plants the successor on camera (agent_sdk.py, 'they support both a Python version and a bun version'). That SDK matured into the Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS): typed messages, sessions, hooks, subagents, structured outputs — production ADWs today start there, while the subprocess form remains the clearest teaching form.

All tac-8 ADWs run agents with permissions fully bypassed (fine for isolated demo repos, risky as a habit). Current practice gates headless agents with allowlists, permission modes, sandboxed bash, and pre/post tool-use hooks — and worktree isolation (which the lesson DOES teach) is now complemented by first-class sandboxing. The lesson's isolation instinct is right; the bypass flag is the dated part.

current_practice_gaps.gap: DIY cron/polling triggers → native background agents, scheduled runs, CI hooks
current_practice_gaps.why: app2/app4 poll with `schedule` loops in long-running terminal processes; app5 hand-rolls a FastAPI server. The trigger CONCEPT is timeless, but current tooling offers headless CI invocation, background tasks, scheduled cloud agents, and webhook-native integrations out of the box — a modern reader should map 'trigger' to those services rather than assume a hand-rolled poller is required.

current_practice_gaps.gap: One serial agent per task → first-class parallel subagents and orchestration
current_practice_gaps.why: tac-8 achieves parallelism at the OS level: detached subprocesses per task, one Claude instance each, coordinated by markdown/Notion state. Current tools offer in-band multi-agent primitives (subagents, parallel tool fan-out, worktree-isolated background agents, orchestration frameworks), so the lesson's parallel patterns can now be expressed inside the agent runtime itself — same architecture, less scaffolding.

Scripts toggle sonnet|opus of the course era; the app5 start script hard-codes Dan's local claude path; the Notion MCP server and .mcp.json format are course-era versions. All incidental: swap in current model names/paths and everything runs. Dan future-proofs this explicitly ('tools will change and models will improve — we can't fixate').

app5's agent-embedded-application (SQLite session store + resume + in-app chat windows) is a hand-built preview of what the Agent SDK now supports directly: embedding long-lived, session-resuming agents into products. The 'outside the loop is inside the application' idea has gone from demo to standard architecture.
